title: Write a custom `@FunctionalInterface` with a method `boolean test(Employee e, double threshold)` and use it as a lambda.
shortTitle: Write a custom @FunctionalInterface with boolean test(Employee e, double threshold) and use it as a lambda

s1_definition.profdef: A `@FunctionalInterface` is an interface with exactly one abstract method, which can be implemented by a lambda. A custom one with `boolean test(Employee e, double threshold)` captures a two-argument predicate that the built-in `Predicate` and `BiPredicate` do not express as naturally.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya invents her own yes-or-no rule form that takes an employee and a threshold amount. Because the form has exactly one blank to fill, she can fill it with a one-line lambda.
s1_definition.oneliner: A single-abstract-method interface annotated `@FunctionalInterface` can be implemented by a lambda — define your own when the built-ins do not fit.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A `@FunctionalInterface` is an interface with exactly one abstract method, which can be implemented by a lambda. A custom one with `boolean test(Employee e, double threshold)` captures a two-argument predicate that the built-in `Predicate` and `BiPredicate` do not express as naturally.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya invents her own yes-or-no rule form that takes an employee and a threshold amount. Because the form has exactly one blank to fill, she can fill it with a one-line lambda.

**One line to remember:** A single-abstract-method interface annotated `@FunctionalInterface` can be implemented by a lambda — define your own when the built-ins do not fit.

sections.s2_technical:
The `@FunctionalInterface` annotation tells the compiler to enforce exactly one abstract method, so adding a second would be a compile error. Declaring `interface SalaryCheck { boolean test(Employee e, double threshold); }` lets you write `SalaryCheck earnsMoreThan = (e, t) -> e.getSalary() > t`, a two-argument boolean test tailored to your domain.

Although `BiPredicate<Employee, Double>` could work, a named custom interface reads better, avoids boxing the double, and documents the intent — "a salary check" is clearer than a generic BiPredicate. You then call it as `earnsMoreThan.test(employee, 50_000)`.

The senior nuance is when to create a custom functional interface versus reuse a built-in. I create one when it improves readability, avoids autoboxing on a primitive, or needs a domain-specific name; otherwise I reuse `Predicate`, `Function`, and friends to keep the codebase conventional. The annotation is a safety net — it is optional for a lambda to work, but it prevents someone from accidentally breaking the single-method contract later.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India needs a clearly-named, primitive-friendly rule that tests whether an employee's salary exceeds a threshold, reused across several screening rules.

This is exactly what a custom functional interface does — SalaryCheck names the two-argument boolean test and takes a primitive double threshold without boxing.

The code defines the `SalaryCheck` interface and a `ScreeningService` using it.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: Rajesh 1,000,000 and Amit 40,000, with a threshold of 50,000.

Step 1: The lambda implements SalaryCheck's single test method as salary greater than threshold.

Step 2: screen filters each employee by calling check.test with the employee and the threshold.

Step 3: Rajesh at 1,000,000 passes; Amit at 40,000 fails.

Step 4: The surviving names, just Rajesh, are collected.

```
INFO: Passed screening (salary > 50000): [Rajesh]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  SalaryCheck earnsMoreThan = (e, t) -> e.getSalary() > t   ← lambda implements SAM
       │
       ▼
  [Rajesh/1M, Amit/40k] + threshold 50k
    │ filter(check.test(e, 50000))
    ▼
  [Rajesh]
```

  │ staff    │→│ ScreeningService │

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — custom @FunctionalInterface ═══

  ┌─ single abstract method (SAM) ─────────────────────────────┐
  │ @FunctionalInterface enforces EXACTLY one abstract method  │
  │ boolean test(Employee e, double threshold) ← primitive, no box│
  │ lambda implements the SAM: (e, t) -> e.getSalary() > t     │
  │ prefer custom when: readability, primitive, domain name    │
  │ else reuse Predicate/BiPredicate/Function (conventional)   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────────┐
  │   <<FunctionalInterface>>     │   │   ScreeningService   │
  │   SalaryCheck                 │◀──│ filter(check.test)   │
  │   + test(Employee, double)    │   └──────────────────────┘
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  Call chain:
  1. SalaryCheck via lambda
  2. filter(e -> check.test(e, threshold))
  3. map(getName).toList()
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A functional interface is an interface with exactly one abstract method, which means it can be implemented by a lambda, and the at FunctionalInterface annotation asks the compiler to enforce that single-method rule. When I need a two-argument boolean test that takes an employee and a primitive threshold, I declare my own interface SalaryCheck with a single test method and implement it with a one-line lambda such as employee comma threshold to salary greater than threshold.

The built-in BiPredicate of Employee and Double could technically do this, but a named custom interface reads better, avoids boxing the primitive double, and documents the intent — at the National Bank of India a SalaryCheck is clearer than a generic BiPredicate, and I pass it into a screening service so the rule is a swappable policy.

The senior point I stress is knowing when to create a custom functional interface versus reuse a built-in. I create one when it genuinely improves readability, avoids autoboxing on a primitive, or deserves a domain-specific name; otherwise I reuse Predicate, Function, and the standard set to keep the codebase conventional. The annotation itself is a safety net: a lambda works without it, but it stops someone from later adding a second abstract method and silently breaking the contract.
